title: Agent Plugins Are Maintained Software, Not Write-Once Config
hook: An empirical sweep of 2,018 Claude Code plugin marketplaces found prose instruction files and their scripts drift out of sync — a maintenance dependency traditional software doesn't have.
key_points: Studied 1,926 repositories hosting plugin marketplaces: 8,351 plugins, 77,773 commits across 2,018 marketplaces.
Plugin-touching commit activity grew 8.8x over the six months after the October 2025 launch.
Software-engineering tasks account for 61.3% of all plugins.
Development is feature-driven: feature commits run at more than twice the rate of conventional open-source software (39.6% vs 17.2%).
Inside skills directories, natural-language instruction files and their implementation scripts co-evolve above chance, with 78% of co-changes functionally coupled.
Most other component types evolve independently, and four commit types (docs, perf, style, refactor) carry different meanings here than in ordinary repos.
content_html: Coding agents are increasingly extended through plugin marketplaces, but plugins are not ordinary packages: they deliver functionality through a mix of natural-language instruction files, scripts, and configuration. Hereiz and colleagues ask whether these are maintained artifacts that co-evolve, or one-off files written once and forgotten, and answer it empirically across 1,926 repositories hosting Claude Code plugin marketplaces — 8,351 plugins and 77,773 commits.
extra_html:
What the data shows

The ecosystem is expanding fast: plugin-touching commit activity grew 8.8x over the six months following the October 2025 launch, with software-engineering tasks accounting for 61.3% of plugins. Development skews heavily toward features, at 39.6% feature commits versus 17.2% in conventional open-source software, and the authors note that docs, perf, style, and refactor commits carry substantially different meanings in these repositories than in traditional ones.

The finding that generalizes

Most component types evolve independently — but inside skills directories, natural-language instruction files and their implementation scripts co-change at above-chance rates, with 78% of those co-changes functionally coupled. That is a maintenance dependency between prose and code with no counterpart in traditional software engineering, and a concrete argument for reviewing a skill's instructions and its scripts together. Method and full breakdown in the paper.

related.title: Claude Agent Skills
related.hook: Agent Skills package instructions, scripts, and resources into folders an agent loads on demand — composable, portable expertise, later opened as a standard like MCP.

related.title: Early Adoption of Agentic Coding Tools by GitHub Projects
related.hook: 25,264 agent-written pull requests later: most open-source projects have barely touched agentic coding tools, and the ones that have still keep exactly one human gatekeeping every PR.

related.title: The Regression Tax on Agent Skills
related.hook: Handing an agent a procedural skill doesn't only add wins — it also breaks tasks it used to solve. The best skills win by regressing less, not by gaining more.

flashcards.prompt: How does commit activity in agent plugin repositories compare to conventional open-source software?

choices.text: Far more feature-driven — 39.6% feature commits versus 17.2% in conventional OSS
Almost identical, suggesting plugins are maintained like ordinary packages
Dominated by refactor commits, since prose files are rewritten constantly

flashcards.explanation_html: Plugin development skews heavily toward adding features rather than the maintenance mix typical of conventional OSS.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the paper argue agent plugins deserve their own study?
flashcards.back_html: They deliver functionality through a mix of natural-language instruction files, scripts, and config rather than source code alone — so traditional maintenance findings may not transfer.
